name: Silky Hayauchi 390mm Replacement Blade
title: Silky Hayauchi Replacement Blade 390mm
meta: Silky Hayauchi replacement blade, 390mm curved pole saw blade for crews pruning from the ground. Fit notes, swap steps and when a new blade beats sharpening.
tagline: A fresh 390mm curved blade to put a tired Hayauchi pole saw back on the job.
summary: The Silky Hayauchi replacement blade is the 390mm curved saw blade that bolts onto the Hayauchi telescoping pole saw. When the teeth go dull, a tooth chips on a hidden nail or the blade takes a kink, a new blade brings the saw back to how it cut on day one.
highlights: 390mm (about 15.4 in) curved pull-stroke blade
Made for the Silky Hayauchi pole saw
Hardened teeth that are meant to be replaced, not filed
Curve keeps the teeth biting on overhead cuts
Bolt-on swap with the saw's own hardware

body.h: Why crews keep a spare Hayauchi blade
p: The Hayauchi is the pole saw a lot of crews reach for when they need reach without a powered pole pruner: clearance pruning over sidewalks, lifting canopies over driveways, cleaning deadwood out of a lower crown from the ground. The pole does the reaching, but the blade does the work, and the 390mm blade is the part that wears out.

Silky hardens its teeth so they stay sharp a long time, which is great until they are finally done. Hardened teeth are not something you touch up with a file in the truck. Once the saw starts skating instead of biting, or you feel it bind and drift in a cut it used to rip through, it is time for a new blade. A spare in the truck turns a dead saw into a two-minute fix.

body.h: What the 390mm curve does on the job
p: The curve matters on a pole saw. When you are pulling down and back on a limb above your head, a straight blade tends to ride out of the kerf. The Hayauchi's curved blade keeps the teeth pulled into the wood, so each stroke takes a full bite with less wasted effort and less wobble at the top of a long pole.

At 390mm the blade handles the limbs you would normally take with a pole saw, from small suckers to wrist-thick laterals, with enough length for a long, efficient stroke. For bigger wood, make a small undercut first so the limb does not tear bark down the stem, then finish from the top. Keep yourself and anyone else out from under the drop zone, and never use any pole tool near energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist with the right equipment.
Pole saw cuts reward patience. Let the teeth do the work with long, smooth strokes rather than short, hard jabs, which wear the blade faster and shake the pole.

Lay the saw down on a flat surface with the blade fully closed out of the way of your hands. Remove the blade bolt and nut from the head, lift the old blade off, set the new one in the same orientation and snug the hardware back down. Check that the blade sits fully seated and does not rock before you extend the pole.

Wear gloves while you handle the bare blade, the teeth are sharp enough to open a hand in one careless move. Wrap the old blade in tape or cardboard before it goes in the trash so nobody gets cut on the way to the dumpster.

body.h: Keeping a new blade cutting longer
p: Wipe sap off the blade at the end of the day and give it a light coat of oil before it goes back in the scabbard or truck rack. Pitch build-up makes any saw drag. Avoid cutting into the ground, wire, or old hardware buried in the wood; one nail can take out several teeth in a single stroke.
Browse more saw and pole saw blades in our replacement blades section, and make sure the blade you order matches the length of the head on your saw.

faq.q: Can I sharpen a Silky Hayauchi blade?
faq.a: Silky teeth are hardened and are not designed to be filed. When the blade stops cutting well, replace it rather than trying to sharpen it.

faq.q: Will a 390mm blade fit other Silky pole saws?
faq.a: Silky blades are specific to each saw model and length. Match the replacement to your saw's model and blade length before you order.

faq.q: How do I know it is time for a new blade?
faq.a: If the saw skates, binds, drifts off line or needs noticeably more effort on cuts it used to handle easily, or if teeth are chipped or the blade is bent, swap it.

name: Petzl Flow 11.6 mm Climbing Rope
title: Petzl Flow 11.6 mm Arborist Climbing Rope
meta: Petzl Flow 11.6 mm climbing rope for tree work: a smooth semi-static line that runs well in the Zigzag and other mechanical devices for DdRT and SRT climbs.
tagline: A smooth, firm 11.6 mm tree climbing line built to pair with Petzl's mechanical prusiks.
summary: The Petzl Flow 11.6 is a semi-static arborist climbing rope designed to run with Petzl's ZIGZAG and ZIGZAG PLUS mechanical prusiks and other modern climbing systems. It is a firm, round line with a tough sheath that feeds cleanly through hardware and holds up to bark, which is why many climbers who run a Zigzag pair it with Flow.
highlights: 11.6 mm diameter, sized for mechanical prusiks and hitches
Semi-static kernmantle build for low stretch on the climb
Designed with the Petzl ZIGZAG family in mind
Usable in both moving rope (DdRT) and stationary rope (SRT) systems
Firm, round hand that tends spliced eyes and feeds hardware well

p: Rope choice is really device choice. The Flow 11.6 was built by Petzl to work with its own mechanical prusiks, so if you climb on a ZIGZAG or ZIGZAG PLUS, it is the line the device was tuned around. That shows up as predictable friction on the descent, smooth tending as you move up and around the canopy, and fewer surprises when the rope gets wet or dirty.

At 11.6 mm it also sits in the sweet spot for most arborist hitches and devices that call for an 11 to 13 mm line. Always check your specific device's manual for the rope range it was tested on before you pair them; the manufacturer's list is the one that counts.

Firm ropes also hold a spliced eye well, so many climbers have one end spliced to work with a mechanical device or a hitch climber setup, which saves tying and dressing a termination knot every morning.

body.h: How it handles on a real climb
p: On a moving rope setup the Flow feeds through a friction saver or around a limb with less drag than a fuzzy, soft line, and its firm sheath keeps a hitch or device from biting too hard. Climbers who work SRT will notice the low stretch on the way up, with less bounce when you are hip-thrusting or using a foot ascender to gain height.

The sheath is tight and abrasion resistant, which matters when you are pulling the line through rough bark, over a basal anchor or across a cambium saver all day. Like any kernmantle rope, it will glaze and fuzz over time, and the way it feels in your device will change as it wears.

Expect a short break-in period. A new kernmantle rope can feel slick and run a bit fast through a device until the sheath settles, so set friction on the conservative side for the first few climbs and adjust as it beds in.

Your climbing line is life-support gear. Use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturers' instructions, and only after proper training. Inspect the full length before each climb by running it through your hands and looking for cuts, glazing, soft or stiff spots, core showing through the sheath, or chemical and saw damage.

Store it clean and dry in a rope bag away from fuel, bar oil and sunlight. Keep a log of its age and use, and retire it immediately after a severe load, a saw nick, or any damage you cannot rule out. When in doubt, cut it up and buy a new one.

Pick a length that is at least twice your working height for moving rope climbing, and long enough to reach the ground from your highest tie-in for SRT, plus extra for tails and a rescue. Many climbers keep a long line for big removals and a shorter one for quick prunes. See more lines in our 24-strand and kernmantle climbing rope range.
If you are building a new setup, buy the rope and the device together so you can test them as a pair, and record the purchase date and length in your gear log the day it arrives.

faq.q: Does the Petzl Flow work with devices other than the ZIGZAG?
faq.a: It is in the diameter range many arborist devices and hitches use, but compatibility is set by each device maker. Check the device manual's approved rope list before you climb on any combination.

faq.q: Can I use the Petzl Flow for SRT?
faq.a: Yes, it is designed for tree climbing in both moving rope and stationary rope systems, as long as your devices and anchor setup are rated for that use.

faq.q: How long will the Flow last?
faq.a: It depends on how often you climb and how you treat it. Inspect it before every use and retire it on damage, heavy wear or after the manufacturer's maximum service life.

name: Husqvarna X-COM Active Helmet-Mounted Communication System
title: Husqvarna X-COM Active Helmet Communication System
meta: Husqvarna X-COM Active puts crew talk, phone calls and active hearing protection on your helmet so climbers and ground crew stay connected over the saw.
tagline: Helmet muffs with built-in crew talk, so climber and ground can hear each other.
summary: The Husqvarna X-COM Active is a helmet-mounted communication system that combines hearing protection with wireless headset-to-headset talk and a Bluetooth link to your phone. It lets the climber and the ground crew talk in normal voices over a running saw or chipper instead of yelling, waving and guessing.
highlights: Helmet-mounted ear muffs with integrated communication
Headset-to-headset crew talk for climber and ground
Bluetooth connection for phone calls
Active, level-dependent listening so you still hear voices and warnings
Rechargeable battery for a full day on the job
specs: Helmet slot mount; check fit to your helmet

body.h: Why crew comms change the job
p: Most close calls on a tree job start with a miscommunication. A climber calls for a slack line and the ground hears tension. Someone steps into the drop zone because they did not hear "headache" over the chipper. The Husqvarna X-COM Active is built to fix that by putting a radio link right inside your hearing protection.

With every crew member on a headset, the climber can talk a groundie through a rigging cut, ask for a tool on the tag line, or call a pause, all without shouting. The ground crew can warn the climber about a car pulling in or a pedestrian walking under the work. Clear, normal-voice communication is quicker, calmer and safer than hand signals alone.

It is also simply less tiring. A full day of shouting over saws and hand-signaling through branches wears on a crew, and calm, clear talk keeps people focused on the cut in front of them rather than on figuring out what someone meant.

Under the electronics, the X-COM Active is still a set of ear muffs. Active listening lets quiet sounds like voices through at a safe level while still damping the loud noise from saws, chippers and stump grinders. That means you are not pulling a muff off to hear someone, which is when hearing damage happens.

A headset only protects you if the cups seal against your head. Keep the cushions in good shape, replace them when they harden or crack, and check that glasses arms or hats are not breaking the seal. Wear the muffs whenever the saw or chipper is running, not just for the big cuts.
Muffs that pass voices through also help with situational awareness on roadside jobs, where you need to hear traffic, horns and the flagger as well as your crew.

The system mounts to the helmet's accessory slots in place of standard helmet muffs. Confirm your helmet is compatible before ordering, and fit the cups so they sit squarely over your ears without pushing the helmet off level. Pair each headset with the rest of the crew at the start of the day, and pair your phone if you want to take calls in the bucket or on the rope.

Charge the batteries every night. A dead headset in the middle of a removal puts you right back to hand signals, so agree on a backup set of signals and use them if the link drops. Communications gear supports a good crew plan; it does not replace one.
Keep chatter disciplined. Agree on short, standard calls for things like "stand clear", "slack", "tension" and "all clear" so the important messages are not lost in conversation.

It suits climbing crews doing removals and rigging, bucket truck crews working with a spotter, and anyone running a busy site where the climber and ground need to coordinate all day. See more headsets and radios in our other climbing gear section.
It is also a good fit for training new climbers, since a lead climber or trainer on the ground can coach them through each step in real time.

faq.q: Does the X-COM Active work with any helmet?
faq.a: It is designed to mount in helmet accessory slots. Fit varies by helmet, so check compatibility with your specific helmet model before buying.

faq.q: Can I still hear the saw and my surroundings?
faq.a: The active listening feature passes quieter sounds such as voices through while reducing loud noise, so you stay aware without taking the muffs off.

faq.q: Does every crew member need a headset?
faq.a: Yes. Crew talk works between headsets, so each person who needs to be on the conversation needs their own unit.

name: Arbortec Patriot BreatheFlex Pro Chainsaw Pants
title: Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro Chainsaw Pants (Patriot)
h1: Arbortec Patriot BreatheFlex Pro Chainsaw Pants
meta: Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro chainsaw pants in the Patriot version: stretchy, vented saw protection built for climbers and ground crew who move all day.
tagline: Stretchy, vented chainsaw pants for climbers who hate wearing chaps over their gear.
summary: The Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro chainsaw pants are lightweight, stretch-panel saw trousers with cut-resistant protection built into the front of the legs. The Patriot version is the US-market model of the BreatheFlex Pro, made for climbers and ground workers who want saw protection that moves like regular work pants.
highlights: Saw protection built into the pants, no chaps to strap on
Stretch panels for climbing, kneeling and stepping over brush
Vents to dump heat on hot days
Reinforced lower legs where spurs and brush chew fabric
Patriot version made for the US market
specs: Front of legs (check label for coverage)

body.h: Why climbers choose saw pants over chaps
p: Chaps work fine on the ground, but in the tree they snag on stubs, twist on your legs and trap heat. Chainsaw pants like the Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro put the cut-resistant layers inside the pants themselves, so the protection stays where it should when you are working a limb walk, setting a lanyard or crouching in a crotch.

The BreatheFlex Pro is built for movement. Stretch panels in the seat and knees let you high-step onto a limb or drop into a squat without the fabric fighting you, and the overall weight is low enough that you are not dragging extra pounds up the tree on every climb.
Pants also mean you are not wearing a second layer over your work trousers, which helps on hot days and keeps the protection from shifting when your saddle leg loops pull on it.

Heat is the main reason people skip saw protection. Arbortec designs the BreatheFlex line around airflow, with breathable fabric and zip vents you can open when you are sweating through a summer removal. Close them up when the wind picks up or the brush gets thick.

The lower legs get tougher reinforcement, which helps where spurs, rough bark and brush piles wear out ordinary pants. Pair them with good arborist boots and a well-fitted saddle, and the pants should not bunch or ride up under your leg straps.

Pockets and belt loops matter more than you would expect. Check that you can still reach a phone, wedge or file without fighting your saddle, and that braces buttons or a belt keep the pants up when you are hanging in the tree.

body.h: Protection that you have to look after
p: Saw pants only work if the protective layers are intact. The fibers inside are designed to clog a moving chain; once they have been cut, that section is done and the pants should be retired. Inspect them regularly for cuts through the outer fabric, and follow Arbortec's washing instructions, since the wrong detergent or heat can reduce the protection.

Check the label for the standard the pants are certified to and the protected area, and make sure that meets your employer's rules and ANSI Z133 requirements for the work you do. No saw pants are cut proof. Safe saw handling, chain brakes, and training are still your first line of defense.
Keep in mind that most saw protection covers the front of the legs. The back of the leg and other areas are not protected, so good saw technique and body position are still what keeps you safe.

Order by waist and inseam, and try them on with your saddle if you can. You want enough room to move without loose fabric hanging below the boot or catching on gear. Compare other options in our chainsaw pants section.
If you are between sizes, think about what you wear underneath in winter and whether you want a little room for base layers.

faq.q: What does Patriot mean on the BreatheFlex Pro?
faq.a: Patriot is the US-market version of the Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro. Check the label for the specific standard and protection coverage on the pants you buy.

faq.q: Can I wear these instead of chaps?
faq.a: Chainsaw pants are an alternative to chaps when they meet the requirements your employer and ANSI Z133 set for your work. Confirm the certification on the label.

faq.q: What happens if I cut into them?
faq.a: Once the chain reaches the protective layers, that protection is used up. Retire the pants rather than patching them.

faq.q: Are they good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. The stretch panels and lower weight are aimed at climbers who need to move freely in the tree.

name: Stein Modular Guard System
title: Stein Modular Guard System: Stump Grinder Guard
h1: Stein Modular Guard System: Stump Grinder Guard
meta: The Stein Modular Guard System is a portable stump grinder guard that sets up around the work area to catch chips and flying debris near homes, cars and people.
tagline: Portable debris screens that fence in the chip spray when you grind near houses and cars.
summary: The Stein Modular Guard System is a set of free-standing panels that you set up as a stump grinder guard around the cutting area. It knocks down chips, stones and debris thrown by the cutter wheel so you can grind next to windows, siding, fences and parked cars with less risk.
highlights: Free-standing panels that link into a barrier
Configurable around the stump and the grinder
Helps contain chips and thrown debris
Breaks down for transport in the truck or trailer
Useful in tight residential and commercial sites
specs: Stump grinding and similar chip-throwing work
Folds or stacks for the truck
Check listing for panel count and accessories

body.h: Why a stump grinder guard pays for itself
p: A stump grinder's cutter wheel throws chips, soil and stones hard and far. In an open lawn that is a cleanup job. Next to a picture window, a vinyl fence or the customer's truck, it is an insurance claim. A portable stump grinder guard like the Stein Modular Guard System puts a physical barrier between the wheel and anything you cannot afford to break.

It also protects people. Ground crew, homeowners who wander over to watch, and neighbors walking past all benefit from a barrier that catches most of the throw. It does not replace a proper exclusion zone, but it makes the zone easier to manage on tight sites.

A guard also speeds up the job. With less debris flying across the property, there is less cleanup at the end, fewer chips in flower beds and pools, and less time spent explaining dings to a homeowner.

The system is made of separate panels that stand on their own and connect to each other, so you can arrange them to suit the job. Wrap them around three sides of a stump next to a foundation, run a straight wall along a driveway, or close off the side facing the street. Because the panels are modular, you only set up as much as you need.

Position the guard on the side where the throw is heading, which on most grinders is the direction the wheel is cutting. Leave yourself room to sweep the wheel and to step clear of the machine. Recheck the layout every time you move to a new stump or change the side you are cutting from.
On sloped sites, set panels on firm ground and check they cannot tip toward the grinder or a bystander. Wind can catch a panel too, so place them where they will not blow over during the cut.

Even with a guard up, keep bystanders well back, wear eye, face and hearing protection, and follow the grinder manufacturer's instructions for guards and safe distances. Call in utility locates before you grind, and probe for rocks, metal and irrigation lines around the stump. A hidden stone can be thrown with enough force to crack a panel or worse.
Inspect the panels for cracks, bent frames and loose connectors before each job. A damaged panel will not stop debris the way it should, so replace it rather than nursing it along.
Treat the guard as part of your site setup, just like cones and signs, and make setting it up a standard step before the grinder ever starts.

Stump grinding contractors, tree services that grind their own stumps, and municipal crews working near traffic and storefronts all get value from a portable guard. See more equipment for this work in our stump grinding section.
A portable guard is especially useful for crews grinding in urban areas, along fences and next to parked cars where there is no room for a wide exclusion zone.

faq.q: Will a guard stop all thrown debris?
faq.a: No guard stops everything. It reduces how much debris leaves the work area, but you still need eye and face protection and a clear exclusion zone.

faq.q: Can I use it with any stump grinder?
faq.a: It is a free-standing barrier, so it is not tied to one machine. Set it up to suit your grinder's size and the direction it throws debris.

faq.q: How many panels do I need?
faq.a: It depends on how close you work to houses and cars. Check the listing for what comes in the set and add panels if you regularly grind on tight lots.

name: SRS Basal and Canopy Anchors
title: SRS Anchors: Basal and Canopy Anchor Options
h1: SRS Anchor Options: Basal and Canopy
meta: SRS anchor options for tree climbers: basal tie-offs and canopy anchors built from slings, rings and friction savers. How each works and what to look for.
tagline: Slings, rings and hardware that anchor a single rope system at the base or canopy.
summary: An SRS anchor is the point your stationary rope hangs from, either tied off at the base of the tree (basal anchor) or set high in the canopy (canopy anchor). This page covers the slings, rings, friction savers and retrievable setups climbers use to build both, and what to check before you trust one with your weight.
highlights: Basal anchors for retrievable, ground-controlled setups
Canopy anchors for a single tie-in high in the tree
Built from slings, rings, friction savers and connectors
Pairs with a rescue-ready, releasable system on the ground
Choose components rated for life support

p: With a single rope system, your rope stays still and you move on it. The anchor is whatever holds the top of that system. A basal anchor runs the rope up and over a union in the canopy and back down to a tie-off at the base of the tree. A canopy anchor ties or rigs the rope directly to the tree high up, usually around a stem with a sling or a cambium saver.

Basal setups are popular because they are retrievable and can be rigged to release from the ground, which makes rescue and retrieval easier. The tradeoff is that the load at the redirect over the limb can be close to double your weight, so the union you choose has to be sound and the right size. Canopy anchors put less load on the union but you have to climb to install them or isolate them carefully with a throw line.
Many climbers mix both. They may ascend on a basal anchor to get into the tree, then set a canopy anchor or move to a moving rope system for the work itself.

body.h: What goes into an SRS anchor
p: Most anchors are built from a handful of parts: a sling or eye-to-eye loop that goes around the stem, a ring or carabiner to connect the climbing line, and often a friction saver to protect the bark and the rope. Ground-based basal setups add a releasable hitch or device at the base and a second connector for the tail.

Pick components that are rated for life support and that match each other: ring sizes that pass the hardware you need, slings long enough for the stem diameter, and connectors that load along their major axis. Avoid mixing gear when you are not sure how the pieces interact.
Keep your anchor kit simple and consistent. When every sling, ring and connector is the same from tree to tree, you build it faster and spot problems sooner.

Every anchor is life-support gear. Use it only as described by the manufacturers, inside a system that meets ANSI Z133, and only after you have been trained to set up and rescue from SRS. Inspect slings for cuts and glazing, rings and connectors for burrs and wear, and look over the tree itself for decay, cracks and dead wood before you commit to an anchor point.

Test every anchor with a bounce test from the ground before you leave it, and plan how you would lower or rescue a climber from it before anyone ascends. A releasable basal setup is a strong habit to build for exactly that reason.
Consider the tree's structure as part of the system. A sound union in a healthy stem is just as important as the rated strength of any hardware you hang from it.

Many climbers carry a dedicated anchor kit: a couple of slings of different lengths, a few rings, a friction saver and spare connectors. Browse anchor hardware and related gear in our climbing gear section.
If you are new to SRS, start with a simple, well-tested setup from a trainer and only add components once you understand what each one does.

faq.q: Is a basal anchor safe for SRS?
faq.a: A properly built basal anchor is a common SRS setup, but the redirect union sees more load than with a canopy anchor. Choose a sound, appropriately sized union and use rated components.

faq.q: Do I need a friction saver for an SRS anchor?
faq.a: It is not always required, but a friction saver or cambium saver protects both the tree and the rope and gives more predictable friction.

faq.q: What makes an anchor releasable?
faq.a: A releasable setup lets someone on the ground lower the climber by releasing the tie-off at the base in a controlled way. Learn and practice it with a qualified trainer.

name: Rope Grabs and Lanyard Adjusters
title: Lanyard Adjusters and Rope Grabs for Fliplines
meta: Lanyard adjuster and rope grab options for arborist fliplines. Compare mechanical adjusters and hitch setups, rope fit, and how to inspect them before use.
tagline: The mechanical adjusters that let you shorten and lengthen a flipline with one hand.
summary: A lanyard adjuster is the rope grab on your flipline that lets you take up slack or let it out without retying a hitch. These devices clamp the lanyard rope under load and slide when you work them, which makes positioning on a spar or around a stem quicker and more controlled.
highlights: One-handed adjustment of flipline length
Mechanical grip holds position under load
Smooth slack tending as you move around the stem
Must match the lanyard rope diameter
Often sold on complete lanyard kits
specs: Match to device's stated diameter range

p: On a spar or a big lead, your flipline holds you in position while you work. The length has to change constantly as you climb up, move around, or lean back for a cut. A lanyard adjuster lets you do that with one hand: pull the tail to shorten, work the device to lengthen. Compared with tending a friction hitch on a lanyard, a good mechanical adjuster is quicker, more consistent, and less likely to creep.
Some climbers still prefer a hitch and pulley for its smoothness and low cost. Mechanical rope grabs win on speed and on not having to tie and dress the hitch every time you set up.
A good adjuster also makes it easy to reach a comfortable lean-back angle, which takes load off your legs and lets you work longer without tiring on a big trunk.

Every rope grab is tested on a range of rope diameters and constructions. Running one on a line that is too thin, too stiff, too slick or worn can make it slip or grab too hard. Check the device manual's rope list and buy the lanyard and adjuster as a matched pair when you can, or as a complete lanyard kit.

Pay attention to how the adjuster attaches to your saddle. Most clip to a side D with a locking carabiner, and the carabiner should be loaded along its spine, not across the gate. Follow the manufacturer's diagram for which end of the device faces the lanyard and which faces the tail.

Some lanyard kits come with the adjuster, rope, snap and swivel already matched and assembled. That takes the guesswork out of compatibility and is a good place to start if you are building your first kit.

On removals, the adjuster lets you snug in tight to the trunk before a cut and back off quickly afterward. On spars with a steel-core flipline for the cut, keep a second point of attachment in place, so that a flipline is never your only connection when a saw is running near it. Practice adjusting under load at ground level before you use a new device aloft.

When you change position around a trunk, keep your hands clear of the device and the rope path. Let the adjuster do its job and move the lanyard around the stem with steady pulls rather than sudden jerks.

Lanyard adjusters are life-support gear. Use them only as part of a system meeting ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and only after training. Check cams, springs and pins for wear, burrs or sticking before each use, keep them clean of sap and grit, and retire any device that has been dropped hard, shock loaded or that does not lock and release cleanly. See matching lanyards in our fliplines and lanyards section.
Replace the lanyard rope when it shows wear even if the adjuster is still fine, and check that the new rope is still within the device's approved range.

faq.q: Can I put any lanyard adjuster on my existing flipline?
faq.a: Only if your rope is within the device's tested diameter and construction range. Check the manual before pairing them.

faq.q: Is a mechanical adjuster better than a hitch?
faq.a: It is quicker and more consistent for most climbers. A hitch and pulley can be smoother and cheaper. Either works when set up and inspected properly.

faq.q: Can I use a lanyard adjuster on a steel-core flipline?
faq.a: Only devices specifically designed for wire-core lanyards. Most rope grabs are made for textile rope only.

name: Rope Runner Pro
title: Rope Runner Pro Mechanical Climbing Device
meta: The Rope Runner Pro is a mechanical friction device for arborists that climbs on both moving and stationary rope, with smooth descent control and easy tending.
tagline: A mechanical friction device for moving rope or SRT with fine descent control.
summary: The Rope Runner Pro is a mechanical friction device for tree climbers that works on both moving rope (MRS/DdRT) and stationary rope (SRS/SRT). It replaces a hitch with an adjustable, bollard-style friction path, giving a smooth descent, quick slack tending and less time spent dressing and setting hitch cord.
highlights: Climbs on both moving rope and stationary rope systems
Adjustable friction for different ropes and climber weights
Smooth, controllable descent
Tends slack easily with a hitch-tending pulley below
No hitch cord to tie or wear out
specs: Check manual for approved diameters and ropes

body.h: What the Rope Runner Pro does
p: The Rope Runner Pro is a mechanical device that takes the place of a friction hitch on your climbing line. The rope runs through a friction path that grips under load and slides when you work the device, so you control your descent with one hand and can set friction to match the rope and your weight. Many climbers move to a device like this to get more consistent feel than a hitch gives, especially as hitch cord wears or the rope gets wet.

The Pro version is set up for both moving rope and stationary rope climbing. That means you can run it on a basal or canopy-anchored SRT line for access, then switch to a doubled moving rope for work positioning, with the same device on your bridge.

Climbers coming from a hitch setup usually notice the difference in how consistent it feels. The device behaves the same in the morning and after lunch, wet or dry, as long as the rope is within its approved range.

In MRS, the device sits on your bridge and the running end comes back through a hitch-tending pulley below it. Pull down on the tail and the device advances; ease the handle and you descend. In SRS, it works as your descent and work-positioning device with a separate ascent system, such as a foot ascender and a handled ascender or a chest rig, depending on your setup.

The real advantage shows up on long days in the canopy. You can set friction a little tighter for long descents and back it off for tending in the crown. It does not glaze or creep the way a worn hitch does, and it does not need retying at the start of each climb.

Mechanical devices are tuned for certain rope diameters and constructions. Use only ropes listed as compatible in the manufacturer's manual, and test friction low to the ground every time you change ropes, as stiffness, coatings, wear and moisture all change how it feels. A rope that is too thin or slick can run faster than you expect.

Install it exactly as the instructions show, with the correct connector and orientation on your bridge. Practice switching between systems, rescue scenarios and changeovers in a training setting before you rely on it at height.
Practice the transition between climbing systems until it is second nature. Being able to change over cleanly and quickly is part of being able to rescue yourself or someone else.

The Rope Runner Pro is life-support equipment. Use it only within a climbing system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and only after training. Before every climb, check moving parts for wear, sharp edges, cracks and smooth operation, and keep it free of sap and grit. Retire it after a fall or impact you cannot rule out, or when wear reaches the limits in the manual. See related devices in our MRS mechanical friction devices section.
Many climbers keep a spare connector and the manual's quick-reference card in their gear bag, so they can check the setup any time they change rope or rebuild the bridge.

faq.q: Can the Rope Runner Pro be used for SRT?
faq.a: Yes, the Pro version is set up for both moving rope and stationary rope climbing when installed and used as the manual describes.

faq.q: What rope does it work with?
faq.a: Use only the ropes and diameters listed as compatible in the manufacturer's manual, and test friction near the ground with any new rope.

faq.q: Do I still need a hitch-tending pulley?
faq.a: For moving rope climbing, a hitch-tending pulley below the device makes slack tending much easier. Follow the manual's recommended setup.

name: Samson Reinforced Tenex 3/8 in Rope
title: Samson Tenex 3/8 in Reinforced Rigging Rope
meta: Samson Tenex 3/8 in reinforced polyester line for light rigging, slings, loopies and tag lines. Easy to splice, firm and abrasion resistant for daily tree work.
tagline: Firm, spliceable 3/8 in polyester line for light rigging, slings and tag lines.
summary: Samson Tenex 3/8 is a 12-strand polyester single braid that tree crews use for light rigging, homemade slings, prusiks, loopies and tag lines. The reinforced version is built for extra abrasion resistance, so it holds up better when dragged through bark and brush.
highlights: 3/8 in 12-strand polyester single braid
Easy to splice with a fid
Low stretch, firm hand
Good for slings, loopies and tag lines
Reinforced for abrasion

p: Tenex is a go-to line for crews who splice their own gear. At 3/8 in it is the right size for eye-to-eye slings, false crotch loopies, light lowering of small wood and pulling lines. The 12-strand braid is simple to bury-splice, so you can make up exactly the lengths you need.

Polyester keeps stretch low and resists sunlight and abrasion better than nylon, which helps a line that lives in the bed of a truck. The reinforced build gives it a bit more toughness when it rubs over bark and stubs.
It also makes a good tag line for steering pieces, and a pull line for setting heavier rigging rope in the tree.

This is light-duty rigging rope. Size your rigging to the load with a healthy safety margin, and never use rigging line for climbing. Shock loads from free-falling wood can be many times the piece's weight, so keep pieces small with 3/8 line.
Inspect for cuts, melted or glazed spots and crushed sections before use, and retire any length that has been shock loaded hard or cut. See heavier lines in our rigging rope section.
Keep it coiled and stored dry and out of direct sun to get the longest life from it.

faq.q: Can I climb on 3/8 Tenex?
faq.a: No. It is a rigging and utility line, not a life-support climbing rope.

faq.q: Is Tenex easy to splice?
faq.a: Yes. Its 12-strand single braid takes a standard bury splice with a fid, which is why crews use it for slings and loopies.

name: Yale Black Beeline 8mm Hitch Cord (by the Foot)
title: Yale Beeline 8mm Hitch Cord, Black, by the Foot
meta: Yale Beeline 8mm hitch cord in black, sold by the foot. A heat-resistant, firm cord climbers tie into Valdotains, Distels and split tails for friction hitches.
tagline: 8mm hitch cord by the foot for climbers who tie and splice their own split tails.
summary: Yale Beeline 8mm is a hitch cord that tree climbers use to tie friction hitches like the Valdotain Tresse and Distel on their climbing line. Sold by the foot in black, it lets you cut exactly the length you need for a split tail, eye-to-eye or prusik.
highlights: 8mm diameter for friction hitches
Sold by the foot, cut to your length
Firm cord that holds a hitch shape
Black color
Built to resist heat from descents

p: A friction hitch is only as good as the cord it is tied with. Beeline is made to grab your climbing line under load, release cleanly when you break the hitch, and handle the heat a fast descent puts into the cord. At 8mm it suits most 11 to 13 mm climbing lines, though the right match depends on your rope's sheath and stiffness.
Buying by the foot means you can cut lengths for a Valdotain, a Distel, a footlock prusik or a spare, and finish the ends with stopper knots or have eyes spliced.
Black hides dirt and pitch better than bright colors, which some climbers like, though it can make wear harder to see, so inspect it closely.

Always test a new hitch cord and rope pairing close to the ground. Too much grip and the hitch is jerky; too little and it creeps. Adjust wraps and braids until it feels right, and dress and set the hitch every time.

Hitch cord is life-support gear and a wear item. Use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it. Replace it when it glazes, stiffens, fuzzes heavily or shows any cuts. Browse other cords in our tech cordage section.
Keep spare cord in your kit so you can retie on the job if a hitch starts to glaze or behave differently.

faq.q: How much Beeline do I need for a split tail?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and your rope. Many climbers cut around 30 in or more for a VT; tie it on the ground, adjust, then trim.

faq.q: Can I splice eyes in Beeline?
faq.a: Eyes in hitch cord should be spliced by a qualified splicer or bought pre-spliced. Otherwise use proper stopper knots.

name: Muffler for Husqvarna 372XP X-Torque Chainsaw
title: Husqvarna 372XP X-Torque Muffler Replacement
meta: Replacement 372XP X-Torque muffler for Husqvarna's pro saw. Restore exhaust flow and spark screen protection on a hard-working bucking saw with a direct swap.
tagline: A direct replacement muffler for the X-Torque version of the 372XP.
summary: This Husqvarna 372XP X-Torque muffler replaces a cracked, loose or worn exhaust on the X-Torque version of the 372XP. A sound muffler keeps exhaust heat directed away from you and the saw, holds the spark arrestor screen in place and keeps the saw running as designed.
highlights: Made for the 372XP X-Torque
Replaces cracked or loose mufflers
Keeps spark screen and exhaust in spec
Bolts on with the saw's mounting hardware

p: The 372XP is a workhorse bucking and felling saw, and mufflers take a beating from heat cycles and vibration. Cracks, broken mounting points, a loose heat shield or a muffler that will not hold a bolt torque are all signs it is time. The X-Torque version uses a different muffler from the older 372XP, so confirm your model before ordering.
Check the spark arrestor screen while you are in there. A clogged screen robs power, while a missing or torn one is a fire risk and may break local rules for working in dry areas.
A damaged muffler can also be louder than normal, which adds to the noise exposure you are already dealing with all day.

Let the saw cool fully. Remove the top cover and the muffler bolts, pull the old muffler and gasket, and clean the exhaust port face. Fit a new gasket if the old one is damaged, mount the new muffler and tighten the bolts evenly to the torque in the service manual. Run the saw and recheck the bolts once it has warmed up and cooled again.
If you are not comfortable working on exhaust parts, take it to a qualified saw shop. More saw parts are in our power equipment parts section.
While the muffler is off, inspect the cylinder exhaust port. Scoring or carbon buildup can point to other problems a saw shop should look at.

faq.q: Does this fit the older non X-Torque 372XP?
faq.a: No. Order the muffler made for your saw's version and check the model plate before buying.

faq.q: Should I replace the gasket too?
faq.a: If the gasket is torn, burnt or brittle, yes. A poor seal lets hot exhaust leak where it should not.

name: Threaded Pole Adaptor
title: Threaded Pole Adapter for Pole Saws and Pruners
meta: Threaded pole adapter that lets you fit pole saw heads and pruner tools to a threaded pole tip. A small part that gets more out of the poles you already own.
tagline: Connects threaded-end tools to your pruning poles so one pole can run more heads.
summary: A threaded pole adapter lets you mount saw heads, pruner heads and other tools to a pole with a threaded tip, or fit threaded tools to a pole system that uses a different connection. It is a simple way to get more use out of the poles already on the truck.
highlights: Joins threaded tools and poles
Lets one pole carry several heads
Small enough to keep in the kit bag
Check thread type before ordering
specs: Check thread size and pole system

p: Pruning poles come with several different connections, and not every saw head or tool matches every pole. A threaded pole adapter bridges that gap. With the right one, you can swap between a pole saw head, a pruner or a hook on the same pole without carrying a second pole set.
That matters when you are working out of a crowded truck or walking a long clearance route. Fewer poles to haul, and less time hunting for the right one.
An adapter is also handy when you buy a new tool and want to keep using the poles you already own, instead of replacing a whole set.

Before ordering, confirm the thread type on your tool and the connection on your pole. A loose or wrong-thread fit can let a head spin or drop while you are working overhead. Thread it on by hand until snug, check for play, and recheck it during the day.

Keep everyone out from under the work zone and never use pole tools near energized lines unless you are qualified for line clearance and the poles are rated for it. See compatible poles in our poles and kits section.
Wipe the threads clean and keep them free of grit so they thread on smoothly without cross-threading.

faq.q: Will this fit my pole?
faq.a: It depends on your pole's connection and your tool's thread. Check both before ordering.

faq.q: Does the adapter make my pole insulated?
faq.a: No. Insulation depends on the pole construction and rating, not the adapter. Treat any pole as conductive unless it is rated and tested.

name: Arb Climber Magazine
title: Arb Climber Magazine for Tree Climbers
meta: Arb Climber Magazine is a print magazine for working tree climbers, with gear talk, technique features and stories from arborists in the trade around the world.
tagline: A print magazine made for tree climbers, about climbing gear, technique and the trade.
summary: Arb Climber Magazine is a print publication written for and about working tree climbers. It covers climbing and rigging technique, gear, competitions and the people in the trade, and makes good reading for the break truck or the off-season.
highlights: Written for working arborists and climbers
Technique, gear and industry features
Print format to keep and pass around
Good for apprentices and seasoned climbers alike

p: Arb Climber Magazine focuses on the climbing side of tree work. Expect articles about new climbing systems and devices, rigging ideas, profiles of climbers and companies, competition coverage and the business of running a crew. It is written by and for people who spend their days in trees.
A magazine is a good way to see how other climbers solve the same problems you face, and to hear about gear before you buy it.
Back issues are worth keeping. Older articles on technique and gear often stay useful long after they were printed, and they make good material for crew training talks.
It is also a way to keep up with how the trade is changing, from new climbing standards to the latest thinking on tree care and safety.

Techniques in any article are a starting point, not a substitute for hands-on training. Try new methods low and slow under a qualified trainer, and always follow ANSI Z133 and your equipment manufacturers' instructions.
For more training reading, see our books and training materials section.
It also makes a good gift for the climber who already has every piece of gear they need.

faq.q: Is Arb Climber Magazine for beginners?
faq.a: It suits both new and experienced climbers. Newer climbers should pair what they read with hands-on training.

faq.q: Is this a single issue or a subscription?
faq.a: Check the listing for whether it is a single issue or subscription option.

name: Samson Tenex 3/8 in Hand-Spliced Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: Samson Tenex Prusik, 3/8 in Hand-Spliced Eye-to-Eye
meta: Samson Tenex prusik in 3/8 in polyester with hand-spliced eyes on both ends. Use it for rigging hitches, false crotches and quick tie-ins around the job site.
tagline: A hand-spliced 3/8 in Tenex eye-to-eye for rigging hitches and utility tie-ins.
summary: This Samson Tenex prusik is made from 3/8 in Tenex polyester with a spliced eye on each end. Crews use it as a rigging prusik, to set a quick false crotch or block, to tie off a tag line, or anywhere a short spliced sling with two eyes makes the job faster.
highlights: 3/8 in Samson Tenex polyester
Hand-spliced eye on each end
Firm, abrasion-resistant braid
Handy for rigging hitches and tie-ins

body.h: How crews use a Tenex eye-to-eye
p: A short eye-to-eye is one of those pieces you end up using all day. Tie a prusik onto a rigging line to grab it for a haul, girth a stem to hang a small block, or set a quick redirect. Tenex is firm and holds its shape, so hitches are easy to set and release, and spliced eyes are stronger and neater than knots.
Because Tenex is polyester, it does not stretch much and stands up to sun and abrasion better than many nylon cords.
Spliced eyes also make it easy to clip to a carabiner or girth around a stem without any knots to inspect or untie at the end of the day.

Use this as a rigging and utility prusik unless the maker marks it for climbing. If you use any eye-to-eye as life support, it must be rated for that use, and use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it.
Retire it if the eyes or splices show wear, cuts or pulled strands. See other lengths in our eye-and-eye prusiks section.
Keep a couple of eye-to-eyes on the truck so you always have one handy for rigging hauls and tie-offs.

faq.q: Can I climb on a Tenex eye-to-eye?
faq.a: Only if it is specifically rated and marked for life-support climbing. Otherwise use it for rigging and utility work.

faq.q: Why choose spliced eyes over knots?
faq.a: Spliced eyes are stronger than most knots, sit flatter and do not come untied.

name: Jameson 10 ft Foam-Filled Fiberglass Pole
title: Jameson Foam Filled Pole, 10 ft Fiberglass
meta: Jameson foam filled pole, 10 ft fiberglass section for pole saws and pruners. Light, stiff and made for daily ground pruning and clearance work by tree crews.
tagline: A 10 ft fiberglass pole section with a foam core for pole saws and pruner heads.
summary: The Jameson foam filled pole is a 10 ft fiberglass pole section that tree crews use with pole saws and pruner heads for ground-based pruning. The foam core helps keep moisture and debris out of the tube, and fiberglass gives a stiff, durable pole that stands up to daily truck life.
highlights: 10 ft fiberglass pole section
Foam-filled core
Stiff for controlled overhead cuts
Works with Jameson pole saw and pruner heads
Connects with other sections for more reach

p: A hollow pole can collect moisture and dirt inside the tube. Filling it with foam helps keep that out and keeps the pole consistent over time. Fiberglass also takes knocks better than aluminum and does not dent when it rattles around in the truck.
At 10 ft, this section is long enough to reach most lower canopy work from the ground on its own, and it connects to other sections when you need more reach.
A stiff pole matters on longer reaches. Less flex means more of your effort goes into the cut, and the saw head tracks where you aim it.
Fiberglass is also more forgiving in cold weather than aluminum, which can feel freezing in the hands on winter jobs.

Even foam-filled fiberglass should be treated as conductive unless the pole is specifically rated and tested for electrical work, and only qualified line-clearance arborists should ever work near energized conductors. Keep the pole clean and dry, since dirt and moisture on the surface reduce any insulating value.
Inspect for cracks, splits and worn fittings before use. Keep people out from under the work. See matching saw heads and poles in our poles and kits section.
Store poles off the truck bed floor where they will not be crushed or scratched by other gear.

faq.q: Can I use this pole near power lines?
faq.a: Only qualified line-clearance workers using poles rated and tested for that work should go near energized lines. Treat this pole as conductive.

faq.q: Will it fit my pole saw head?
faq.a: It uses Jameson's pole connection system. Check that your head or adapter matches before ordering.

name: Jobsite Hauling Tarp
title: Jobsite Hauling Tarp for Brush and Debris
meta: A heavy-duty hauling tarp for dragging brush, leaves and debris across lawns to the chipper. Saves trips, protects turf and speeds up cleanup on tree jobs.
tagline: A heavy-duty drag tarp for moving brush and debris across the lawn in one trip.
summary: A hauling tarp is a heavy-duty sheet with handles that lets your ground crew pile brush, leaves and small wood on it and drag the whole load to the chipper or truck. It cuts down on trips, keeps debris off turf and makes the final cleanup much faster.
highlights: Drag full loads of brush in one trip
Handles for one or two people
Protects lawns from scuffing and debris
Rolls up small for the truck
specs: Brush, leaves, small wood and debris

p: On a pruning job, cleanup can take as long as the climbing. A hauling tarp turns a dozen armloads into one drag. Lay it under the work area, let the climber drop small brush right on it, then pull the whole pile to the chipper. It also works for raking leaves, hauling stump grindings and moving debris out of backyards with narrow gates.
Because the load slides on the tarp instead of being dragged across the grass, you leave less damage and fewer twigs in the turf.
A tarp is also handy as a ground cover for gear and tools, and to catch sawdust and debris near patios and pools.

Do not overload it. A tarp piled too high gets hard to pull and puts a strain on your back and on the handles. Pull with your legs, keep a straight back, and use two people for heavy loads. Keep the tarp clear of the chipper infeed so it cannot be pulled in.
Shake it out and let it dry before rolling it up to stop mildew. More cleanup gear is in our landscaper tools section.
Check the handles and seams for wear and replace the tarp when the fabric starts to tear, so it does not fail mid-drag.
Some crews keep two tarps: one for active brush hauling and one for clean jobs, like laying tools out or protecting a patio.

faq.q: Can I drop brush on the tarp from above?
faq.a: Yes, for small brush. Keep people out of the drop zone and do not drop heavy wood on it.

faq.q: How do I clean it?
faq.a: Shake it out, hose it off if needed, and let it dry before storage.

name: New England Ropes Accessory Cord
title: New England Accessory Cord, Sold by the Foot
meta: New England accessory cord by the foot: nylon kernmantle cord for gear loops, tool tethers, tie-offs and utility jobs around the truck and the climbing kit.
tagline: Kernmantle utility cord by the foot for tethers, gear loops and tie-offs.
summary: New England accessory cord is a nylon kernmantle utility cord sold by the foot in several diameters. Arborists use it for tool tethers, gear loops on saddles and bags, tie-offs, and general rigging of non-life-support items around the job.
highlights: Nylon kernmantle construction
Sold by the foot
Several diameters available
Good for tethers, gear loops and tie-offs

body.h: Utility cord for the truck and the tree
p: Every kit needs some good cord. Accessory cord is handy for tool lanyards on handsaws and pruners, loops to hang gear on your saddle, tie-downs for bags and pole saws on the truck, and drawstrings on rope bags. The kernmantle build holds knots well and is easy to handle.
Buying by the foot means you can cut exactly what you need instead of buying a whole spool.
It is also good for making up quick throw bag pouches, holding a rope bag shut, or tying a pole saw to the truck rack.
Pick the diameter that suits the job: thinner cord for light tethers and gear loops, thicker cord for tie-downs and anything you want to grip easily.

Accessory cord is not climbing rope or hitch cord unless the specific product is rated and marked for that use. Do not use it for life support, and do not use it as rigging for wood. Melt or tape the cut ends to stop fraying, and tie secure knots.
Replace cord that is fuzzed, cut or stiff. For hitch cords and climbing-rated cordage, see our tech cordage section.
Keep a hank of cord in your gear bag; it is one of those things you will reach for on almost every job.

faq.q: Can I use accessory cord as a prusik for climbing?
faq.a: Only if the specific cord is rated for that use. Most accessory cord is for utility tasks, not life support.

faq.q: How do I stop the ends fraying?
faq.a: Melt the cut end carefully with a flame or hot knife, or wrap it tightly with tape.

name: Buckingham 20 oz Throw Weight
title: Buckingham 20 oz Throw Weight for Big Trees
meta: Buckingham 20 oz throw weight for setting lines in tall trees and thick canopies. A heavier bag that pulls throw line down through bark and small branches.
tagline: A heavy 20 oz throw bag for setting lines in big, tall or thick canopies.
summary: The Buckingham 20 oz throw weight is a heavy throw bag for arborists who need to set a line high in big trees or through dense canopy. The extra weight helps it drop back to the ground through twigs and over rough bark that would hang up a lighter bag.
highlights: 20 oz weight for tall trees
Pulls line down through thick canopy
Ring for attaching throw line
Bright color to spot on the ground

p: Most climbers carry a range of throw weights. Light bags are easier to throw high and accurately, but they can hang up in small branches or fail to pull line back down over a rough union. A 20 oz throw weight is the one you grab when the line refuses to come down, in tall conifers or big oaks with a lot of small wood.
The extra weight also makes it easier to isolate a union by shaking the line, and works well with a big shot slingshot when you need serious height.
If you work in big hardwoods or tall pines, a heavy bag in your kit saves a lot of time and frustration.

A 20 oz bag hurts if it hits someone. Clear the area under the tree, call out before each throw, and keep everyone back from where it can fall. Watch out for power lines, and never throw near energized conductors.
Check the bag and ring for wear and replace a bag with torn fabric. See throw lines and more weights in our throw weight and line section.
Store throw weights and line together in a bag or cube so they stay tangle free and ready to use.
Keep the line flaked loosely before each throw so it pays out without snagging the bag.

faq.q: Is 20 oz too heavy for hand throwing?
faq.a: It can be thrown by hand, but many climbers use it with a big shot. Lighter bags are easier for accurate hand throws.

faq.q: What throw line works with it?
faq.a: Use a throw line strong enough for the weight and your launcher. Check the line maker's guidance.

name: Forged Steel Rigging Ring
title: Forged Steel Rigging Ring for Slings and Anchors
meta: Forged steel rigging ring for building ring slings, anchors and redirects in tree rigging. A tough, smooth ring that holds up to daily rigging work.
tagline: A tough forged steel ring for building ring slings, anchors and redirects.
summary: A forged steel rigging ring is a solid ring that tree crews splice or girth into slings to build anchors, redirects and adjustable rigging points. Steel stands up to the wear and abuse of rigging rope running across it day after day.
highlights: Forged steel construction
Smooth surface for rope
For ring slings and redirects
Check the rated strength before use

p: Rings are a simple, strong way to build adjustable anchors. Splice one onto a sling, or pair two rings for a ring-and-ring false crotch. In rigging, rope runs through and across rings constantly, so a forged steel ring holds up better than aluminum when you are lowering wood all day.
Make sure the ring is large enough for the rope and hardware you plan to pass through it, and smooth enough to avoid cutting rope fibers.
Rings also let you change rope direction without the friction and wear that come from running rope directly over bark.

Choose a ring with a working load limit suited to your rigging, allowing for the high forces created when wood is dropped or swung onto a rigging point. Check the marking or listing for its rated strength and do not exceed it.
Inspect rings for nicks, burrs, grooves worn by rope, cracks and deformation before each use, and retire any ring that is damaged. More hardware is in our rings section.
Keep rigging rings separate from climbing hardware so they never end up in a life-support system by mistake.
Clean sap and grit off rings after each job, since grit embedded in a ring will wear rope faster.

faq.q: Can I use a steel rigging ring for climbing?
faq.a: Only if it is rated and marked for life support. Otherwise keep rigging rings for rigging.

faq.q: Why steel instead of aluminum?
faq.a: Steel resists the wear from rope running over it and from rough handling better than aluminum.

name: Yale Polydyne 3/4 in Rigging Rope
title: Yale Polydyne 3/4 in Rigging Rope
meta: Yale Polydyne rigging rope in 3/4 in for lowering big wood on removals. A strong, durable line for heavy rigging with blocks, port-a-wraps and lowering devices.
tagline: Heavy 3/4 in rigging line for big removals and lowering large wood.
summary: Yale Polydyne rigging rope in 3/4 in is a heavy rigging line for lowering big wood on removals. It is sized for rigging blocks and lowering devices that take large rope, and suits crews regularly taking down large trees in pieces.
highlights: 3/4 in diameter for heavy rigging
Made by Yale Cordage
Built for blocks and lowering devices
Durable for daily removal work

p: On big removals, wood gets heavy fast. A 3/4 in rigging line gives the strength and durability for lowering large leaders and trunk sections, and its size grips well on a port-a-wrap or capstan lowering device. Match it with blocks and slings rated for 3/4 in rope and the loads you are working with.
Bigger rope is heavier to carry and set, so many crews keep it for the big jobs and run 1/2 or 5/8 for everyday rigging.
Larger rope also gives the ground crew more to grip and control when they are letting wood run on a lowering device.

Dynamic loads from dropped or swung wood can be several times the piece's weight. Plan your cuts, keep pieces within what your rope, hardware and tree can handle, and let the rope run a little to soften the catch. Keep the ground crew clear of the drop zone and the running line.
Inspect for cuts, glazing, crushed or core-damaged sections before each use. Retire rope after a severe shock load. See more rigging lines in our rigging rope section.
Store the rope clean and dry, out of the sun and away from fuel and chemicals, and keep a log of big removals and severe loads.

faq.q: Can I climb on Polydyne?
faq.a: No. It is a rigging rope, not a life-support climbing line.

faq.q: Will 3/4 in rope fit my rigging block?
faq.a: Check the block's rated rope diameter. Many large blocks take 3/4 in, but smaller ones do not.

name: WestCoast Clutch Cover for Stihl Saws
title: WestCoast Clutch Cover for Stihl Chainsaws
h1: WestCoast Clutch Cover for Stihl Saws
meta: WestCoast clutch cover for Stihl chainsaws: an aftermarket sprocket cover that replaces a cracked or stripped one and keeps the bar clamped and chain guarded.
tagline: A replacement clutch (sprocket) cover from WestCoast Saw for Stihl chainsaws.
summary: This WestCoast clutch cover is an aftermarket replacement sprocket cover for Stihl chainsaws, made by WestCoast Saw. It replaces a cracked, stripped or worn cover so the bar clamps down properly and the clutch and chain stay guarded.
highlights: Replacement Stihl clutch cover
Made by WestCoast Saw
Swap out cracked or stripped covers
Check model fit before ordering

p: The clutch cover takes a beating. It clamps the bar, houses the chain catcher area and often carries the chain brake on some models. Cracks, stripped bar nut studs, a worn chain tensioner or a cover that will not clamp the bar firmly all mean it is time for a new one.
WestCoast Saw makes aftermarket parts for pro saws. Clutch covers are model-specific, so check the listing against your exact Stihl model before you order.
A replacement cover is often cheaper and faster than repairing stripped studs or a cracked casting.

Engage the chain brake if your cover carries it, remove the bar nuts and old cover, and clean out sawdust and oil buildup. Fit the new cover, set chain tension and tighten the bar nuts. Check that the chain brake engages and releases properly before cutting.
If the chain brake is part of the cover and you are unsure about fitting it, have a qualified saw shop do the job. See more saw parts in our power equipment parts section.
Check the chain catcher and bar studs at the same time and replace anything worn.

faq.q: Does this fit all Stihl saws?
faq.a: No. Clutch covers are made for specific models. Confirm compatibility for your saw.

faq.q: Is it an OEM Stihl part?
faq.a: No. It is an aftermarket part made by WestCoast Saw.

name: 2-in-1 Lanyards
title: 2-in-1 Lanyard Options for Arborist Positioning
meta: A 2-in-1 lanyard gives arborists two positioning tools in one: an adjustable flipline that doubles as a second tie-in. How it works and what to check.
tagline: A dual-purpose lanyard that works as a flipline and a second point of attachment.
summary: A 2-in-1 lanyard is a work positioning lanyard set up to serve two roles: an adjustable flipline around a stem and a second point of attachment in the canopy. It cuts down on gear on your saddle while giving you more ways to stay tied in.
highlights: Two positioning roles in one lanyard
Adjustable length
Second tie-in for cuts and limb walks
Less gear on your saddle

p: Most climbers carry a flipline for spar work and a second lanyard for staying tied in when they make cuts or move through the canopy. A 2-in-1 design combines these, usually with snaps or connectors at both ends and an adjuster that lets you use the lanyard around the trunk or clipped to a separate anchor.
That saves weight and clutter on your saddle, and it means one well-maintained piece of gear does the job of two.
Many climbers find a 2-in-1 setup especially handy on limb walks, when they want a second attachment above them without adding another lanyard to the saddle.

Work positioning lanyards are life-support gear. Use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it. When running a saw, always have two points of attachment and keep the saw well away from the lanyard; a steel core flipline is safer when cutting close to it.
Inspect the rope, eyes, snaps and adjuster before each climb and retire any lanyard that has been cut or shock loaded. See all options in our fliplines and lanyards section.
Practice adjusting the lanyard and changing configurations at ground level until you can do it smoothly before using it in the tree.

faq.q: Can a 2-in-1 lanyard replace my climbing line?
faq.a: No. It is for work positioning and as a second attachment, not for primary climbing.

faq.q: What length should I choose?
faq.a: Pick a length that wraps the largest stems you work on with room to lean back. Many climbers choose 10 to 12 ft or longer for big removals.

name: Husqvarna X-Cut .325 Mini .043 Chainsaw Chain
title: Husqvarna .325 Mini Chain, .043 Gauge X-Cut
meta: Husqvarna .325 mini chain in .043 gauge for narrow kerf bars on light pro saws. Fast, smooth-cutting X-Cut chain for pruning, limbing and climbing saws.
tagline: Narrow-kerf .325 mini X-Cut chain for light, fast pro saws.
summary: Husqvarna .325 mini chain in .043 gauge is a narrow-kerf X-Cut chain made for light pro saws that run .325 mini bars. The thinner cut takes less power, so smaller saws cut quicker and smoother, which is ideal for pruning, limbing and climbing saws.
highlights: .325 in mini pitch
.043 in (1.1 mm) gauge
Narrow kerf for faster cutting on smaller saws
Husqvarna X-Cut chain
Order by drive link count for your bar

p: A narrower chain removes less wood on every pass. On a saw with less power, that means the chain keeps its speed in the cut instead of bogging down. Husqvarna's .325 mini chain at .043 gauge suits light pro rear-handle and top-handle saws set up with matching narrow-kerf bars.
It also uses a smaller file, so sharpening is quick. Check your file size in the chain's specs and keep your depth gauges in spec.
Narrow-kerf chain is popular on climbing saws because it keeps a light saw cutting fast without needing more power, which helps when you are working one-handed in awkward positions.

Your bar must be .325 mini pitch with a .043 groove, and the drive sprocket must match too. Count the drive links on your old chain or check the bar marking before ordering. Wrong gauge or pitch will not run safely.
Always run the chain brake, wear chainsaw protective gear, and keep the chain sharp and correctly tensioned. More chain options are in our chainsaw chain section.
Run new chain for a few minutes at low load and recheck tension once it warms up; new chains stretch slightly at first.
Keep a spare loop on the truck so a dull or damaged chain never stops the job.

faq.q: Will .325 mini chain fit a standard .325 bar?
faq.a: Not unless the bar groove is .043. Mini chain needs a matching .043 narrow-kerf bar and sprocket.

faq.q: How do I know how many drive links I need?
faq.a: Count the drive links on your old chain or check the number stamped on the bar.

name: 3M Peltor Hygiene Kit for Optime 105 Ear Muffs
title: 3M Peltor Hygiene Kit for Optime 105 Ear Muffs
h1: 3M Peltor Hygiene Kit for Optime 105 Muffs
meta: 3M Peltor hygiene kit for Optime 105 ear muffs: new ear cushions and foam inserts that restore the seal for saw, chipper and stump grinder work.
tagline: New cushions and foam inserts to bring Optime 105 muffs back to a good seal.
summary: The 3M Peltor hygiene kit for Optime 105 ear muffs replaces the ear cushions and foam inserts. Fresh cushions restore the seal that hearing protection depends on, which wears away fast with sweat, sun and sawdust.
highlights: Replacement cushions and foam inserts
Made for Peltor Optime 105 muffs
Restores the seal for proper noise reduction
Snap-in swap

p: Optime 105 muffs are high-attenuation muffs, but they only protect at their rating if the cushions seal. Hard, cracked or flattened cushions let saw and chipper noise leak in. Swapping them out is cheap compared with the hearing loss that leaks cause over years of work.
Plan on replacing the cushions at least once or twice a year with daily use, or sooner if they harden or split.
Sweat, sun and sawdust all speed up cushion wear, and hot summers can harden them faster than you might think.
Pull the old cushions off the cups, remove the old foam, insert the new foam and press the new cushions on until they snap into place all around. Check that they sit flat and the cups close properly.
Clean cushions with mild soap and water only. More options are in our hearing protection section.
Keep a spare set in the truck so a split cushion never means working without hearing protection.
Store the muffs out of direct sun and avoid crushing the cushions in the truck, which keeps them sealing longer.

faq.q: How often should I replace Optime 105 cushions?
faq.a: When they harden, crack or no longer seal, and at least once or twice a year with daily use.

faq.q: Does it fit other Peltor muffs?
faq.a: Peltor hygiene kits are model specific. Confirm your muff model before ordering.

name: Clogger Ascend Gen 2 Chainsaw Pants (HCB Edition)
title: Clogger Ascend Gen 2 Chainsaw Pants, HCB Edition
h1: Clogger Ascend Gen 2 Chainsaw Pants HCB Edition
meta: Clogger Ascend Gen 2 chainsaw pants, HCB edition: lightweight, stretchy saw protection built for climbers. Fit, comfort and care notes before you buy.
tagline: Light, stretchy chainsaw pants built for climbing arborists.
summary: The Clogger Ascend Gen 2 chainsaw pants are lightweight, stretch saw pants designed for climbing arborists. The HCB edition is a special version of the Gen 2 Ascend, with the same climbing-focused fit and built-in saw protection.
highlights: Climbing-focused chainsaw pants
Stretch fabric for free movement
Lightweight for long days aloft
Built-in cut protection on the front of the legs
specs: Check label for standard and coverage

p: Clogger designed the Ascend line for arborists who spend their day in the tree. The Gen 2 pants are cut to move with you on limb walks, high steps and when you are hanging in your saddle, with stretch where you need it and less bulk than traditional saw pants.
The HCB edition keeps the Gen 2 fit and protection. Check the listing for the colorway and any details specific to this edition.
Lighter saw pants also help on hot days, when heavier gear quickly becomes a reason to skip protection.

Saw pants work by clogging the chain with protective fibers. Once those layers have been cut, that protection is gone and the pants should be retired. Check the label for the certification and coverage, and make sure it meets your employer's rules and ANSI Z133 requirements.
Wash them as Clogger instructs to keep the protective layers effective. No saw protection is cut proof. Compare others in our chainsaw pants section.
Order by waist and length and try them with your saddle on so the leg straps sit comfortably over the protective layers.

faq.q: What does HCB edition mean?
faq.a: It is a special edition of the Ascend Gen 2. Check the listing for its specific color and details.

faq.q: Are Clogger pants good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. The Ascend line is designed specifically around climbing arborists.

name: Footlock Prusiks
title: Footlock Prusiks for Tree Climbers
meta: Footlock prusik loops for tree climbers: eye-to-eye hitch cords used as a safety while footlocking up a rope. How they work, sizing and inspection tips.
tagline: Eye-to-eye prusiks for backing up a footlock ascent.
summary: A footlock prusik is an eye-to-eye hitch cord tied around a doubled or single climbing line as your safety while you footlock up the rope. You slide it up as you climb, and it grabs if you slip or stop to rest.
highlights: Eye-to-eye hitch cord
Acts as a safety while footlocking
Slides up easily, grabs under load
Sized to match your climbing line

body.h: How footlocking with a prusik works
p: Footlocking lets you climb a rope by locking it between your feet and standing up, then reaching up and repeating. The footlock prusik, tied as a prusik or similar hitch around the line and clipped to your saddle, is your safety the whole way up. Advance it as you go, and it holds you if you lose your foot lock.
The cord diameter must match the climbing line so the hitch grabs reliably but slides when you push it up.
Many climbers now use mechanical ascenders or other systems for climbing, but footlocking is still a valuable skill and a quick way up a doubled line.

Footlock prusiks are life support. Use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it. Practice footlocking low with a trainer before trying a full climb, and test the hitch every time you tie it.
Replace a prusik that is glazed, stiff or worn, or that has been heavily loaded in a fall. See more options in our hitch cord and split tails section.
Keep the hitch neat and dressed and push it up with your hand as you climb, so it never gets left behind and loaded with slack.

faq.q: What hitch do I use for footlocking?
faq.a: A Prusik or similar gripping hitch is common. Your trainer can show you a hitch that works with your rope and cord.

faq.q: Can I use a footlock prusik for my climbing hitch?
faq.a: Use cords and hitches recommended for each job. A friction hitch for working in the tree may need a different cord or length.

name: 7/8 in T-Rex Anchor Rigging Sling with XL Ring
title: 7/8 in Adjustable Rigging Sling with XL Ring
h1: 7/8 T-Rex Adjustable Rigging Sling with XL Ring
meta: A 7/8 in adjustable rigging sling with an XL ring for heavy anchor points on removals. Wrap big stems, set blocks and adjust the length right on site.
tagline: Heavy 7/8 in adjustable anchor sling with an oversized ring for big rigging points.
summary: This 7/8 in adjustable rigging sling is built for heavy anchor points on big removals. The oversized XL ring lets the sling choke around large stems and adjust to length, so you can set rigging blocks and redirects without carrying slings in every size.
highlights: 7/8 in rope sling for heavy rigging
XL ring for adjustable chokes
Fits large stems
Anchor for blocks and lowering devices

p: On a big removal, the rigging point has to hold the biggest loads of the job. A heavy 7/8 in sling with an XL ring wraps big trunks and adjusts on site, so you can set a block exactly where you want it without a collection of fixed slings. The large ring passes the sling's own eye and makes adjustments easier.
Use it to hang rigging blocks, anchor lowering devices at the base, or build redirects for big leaders.
Adjustable slings are also easier to set in the tree, since you can wrap and choke them without needing an exact length.

Check the rated strength on the tag or listing, and size every part of the system — rope, block, sling and tree — for the dynamic loads you will create. Keep the ground crew clear of the drop zone and running line.
Inspect for cuts, abrasion and core damage, and check the ring for wear and burrs. Retire a sling after a severe shock load. More slings are in our adjustable slings section.
Keep the sling clean and dry, and store it away from fuel and chemicals that can weaken fibers.

faq.q: Can I use this sling for climbing?
faq.a: No. It is a rigging sling for heavy loads, not a life-support climbing anchor.

faq.q: Why use an XL ring?
faq.a: A larger ring lets the sling adjust and choke more easily around big stems.

name: Felling Dog for Husqvarna 395XP
title: Husqvarna 395XP Felling Dog (Bumper Spike)
meta: Husqvarna 395XP felling dog replacement for a worn or bent bumper spike. Gives your big saw a solid pivot point for bucking and felling large wood.
tagline: A replacement bumper spike for the 395XP to keep the saw pivoting cleanly in big wood.
summary: This Husqvarna 395XP felling dog replaces worn, bent or missing bumper spikes on the 395XP. A sharp, solid felling dog gives you a pivot point against the log, so you can lever the saw through big cuts with less effort and more control.
highlights: Replacement felling dog for the 395XP
Pivot point for bucking and felling
Replaces bent or worn spikes
Bolts on

p: On a big saw like the 395XP, the felling dog does a lot of the work. Set it against the log, and you can pivot the bar through the cut using the saw's weight rather than muscling it. Worn or bent spikes slip, which tires you out and makes the saw harder to control.
Replace the dog as soon as the teeth are rounded off or the plate is bent.
A worn felling dog can also make the saw kick or slip unexpectedly, which makes big cuts harder to control.
On the 395XP, a solid dog is especially important because of the saw's weight and the size of the wood it usually cuts.
With the saw off and cool, remove the bar and chain, undo the bolts holding the old dog, and fit the new one in the same position. Tighten securely and reassemble.
Keep the chain brake working, wear full chainsaw protective gear and watch your stance on big wood. More 395XP parts are in our power equipment parts section.
Check the bolts after the first few tanks of fuel and retighten if needed.

faq.q: Does this fit other Husqvarna saws?
faq.a: It is listed for the 395XP. Check fit for any other model before ordering.

faq.q: Do I need to remove the bar to fit it?
faq.a: Usually yes, to reach the mounting bolts.

name: Yale Ultrex 5/8 in Synthetic Winch Line (per Foot)
title: Yale Ultrex 5/8 in Synthetic Winch Line, per Foot
h1: Yale Ultrex 5/8 in Synthetic Winch Line
meta: Yale Ultrex winch line in 5/8 in, sold by the foot. A strong, lightweight synthetic line to replace steel cable on winches and capstans for tree work.
tagline: Light, strong 5/8 in synthetic winch line to replace steel cable.
summary: Yale Ultrex winch line is a high-strength synthetic rope that replaces steel cable on winches. In 5/8 in, sold by the foot, it gives tree crews a lighter, easier-to-handle line for pulling trees, skidding logs and winching on the job.
highlights: 5/8 in synthetic winch line
Lighter and easier to handle than steel
Sold by the foot
No broken wire splinters
