p: Steel cable is heavy, kinks, and frays into wire splinters that cut hands. A synthetic winch line like Yale Ultrex is much lighter to drag out to the tree, easy to splice, and safer to handle. Many crews switch to synthetic on truck and skid steer winches for exactly these reasons.
Synthetic line also stores less energy when it fails than steel, though any line under tension can still recoil.
It is also easy to splice eyes and repairs in the field, so a damaged section can often be cut out and the line put back into service.

Make sure your winch drum and fairlead are suitable for synthetic line; rough rollers and burrs will chew through it. Keep it away from heat and sharp edges, and use chafe protection where it runs over rough surfaces.
Inspect for cuts, heavy abrasion and melted spots, and keep everyone out of the line of pull. More lines are in our rigging rope section.
Wrap it onto the drum under light tension so it does not bury into itself on heavy pulls.
Replace it when abrasion, heat damage or cuts reduce its strength, and never stand in line with a loaded winch line.

faq.q: Can I put Ultrex on any winch?
faq.a: Check that your drum, fairlead and hardware are suited to synthetic line and free of burrs.

faq.q: Is synthetic line as strong as steel cable?
faq.a: High-strength synthetic lines can match or exceed steel of a similar size. Check the rated strength for your diameter.

name: Prusik Loops
title: Prusik Loops for Climbing and Rigging
meta: Prusik loops for arborists: closed cord loops used for friction hitches, backups and rigging grabs. Sizes, uses and how to inspect them before use on the job.
tagline: Closed cord loops for friction hitches, backups and rigging grabs.
summary: Prusik loops are closed loops of cord, either sewn or tied, that arborists use to tie friction hitches around rope. They serve as backups, rope grabs for rigging hauls, and handy attachment points around the job.
highlights: Closed loop of cord
For prusik and other friction hitches
Rope grabs for rigging and hauling
Choose diameter to match your rope

p: A prusik loop is a basic tool. Tie a prusik onto a rigging line to make a haul grab, use one as a backup on a lowering system, or clip gear to it. Climbers also use loops as part of rescue and progress-capture setups.
Match the loop's cord diameter to the rope: too thin and it grabs too hard; too thick and it slips.
Keep a few loops in different diameters so you always have one that fits the rope you are using.

Only loops rated and marked for life support should ever be used to hold a person. If you use one in a climbing system, use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it.
Replace loops that are glazed, stiff, fuzzed or worn. See hitch cords and eye-to-eyes in our hitch cord and split tails section.
Inspect any sewn bartacks closely for cut or pulled stitching, and check tied loops for a secure, well-dressed knot with long enough tails.

faq.q: Are prusik loops strong enough to climb on?
faq.a: Only if they are rated for life support. Check the label or listing.

faq.q: What size do I need?
faq.a: Pick a cord diameter that grips your rope well; usually several millimeters thinner than the rope.

name: Petzl Treesbee Screwlink Friction Saver
title: Petzl Treesbee Screwlink Friction Saver
meta: Petzl Treesbee screwlink friction saver: a false crotch that protects bark and your climbing line, with a screwlink end for flexible setup in the canopy.
tagline: A Petzl friction saver with a screwlink end for protecting rope and bark.
summary: The Petzl Treesbee is a friction saver, or false crotch, that sets around a branch union to protect both the tree's bark and your climbing rope. The screwlink version uses a screw link connector at one end, giving you flexibility in how you build and attach the setup.
highlights: Friction saver / false crotch
Protects bark and rope
Screwlink connector at one end
Reduces friction for smoother climbing

p: Running your climbing line directly over bark wears both. The bark gets burned and the rope gets fuzzed and glazed. A friction saver like the Treesbee keeps the rope off the union and gives a smoother, more predictable friction for moving rope climbing.
The screwlink end lets you build the setup to suit your system, and the screwlink must be fully closed before use.
A friction saver also makes it easier to pull your rope back down at the end of the climb, since the rope runs through the rings instead of over rough bark.

Choose a solid union that suits the load. The Treesbee is life support. Use it only as part of a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every use, and get trained before you rely on it. Make sure the screwlink is closed and that hardware sits correctly before you weight it.
Retire it if the strap or rope is cut, glazed or worn, or if the hardware shows wear grooves. More options are in our friction savers section.
Store it clean and dry, and check it often when you climb in resinous trees, where sap can build up on the strap and hardware.

faq.q: Can I retrieve the Treesbee from the ground?
faq.a: Friction savers can be set up to retrieve from the ground with the right technique. Learn it from a trainer and follow Petzl's instructions.

faq.q: Do I need to close the screwlink?
faq.a: Yes. Always tighten the screwlink fully before loading it.
